items.title: In, or a subset
items.question: Which are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: You read $\in$ as $\subseteq$. The elements of $S$ are numbers; $\{4\}$ is a set.
You reversed the subset. 6 is in $S$ but not in $\{2, 4\}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For $\in$ look for a listed element; for $\subseteq$ check every element of the left set.

explain.text: 4 is listed, so $4 \in S$, and so $\{4\} \subseteq S$. $\varnothing$ is a subset of every set, vacuously. But $\{4\}$ is not listed in $S$, and $6 \notin \{2, 4\}$.

items.title: A complement on a new diagram
items.prose: In $U = \{1, \dots, 10\}$, $A$ is the primes and $B$ the odd numbers.
items.question: Tap every region of $(A \cap B)^c$.

feedback.correct: Right. Everything except 3, 5 and 7: seven numbers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $A \cap B$, then take everything else in $U$.

byKey.and-c: You tapped $A^c \cap B^c$, which is $(A \cup B)^c$. Outside the overlap is more than outside both circles.
byKey.inter: You tapped $A \cap B$ itself. Its complement is the rest.

explain.text: $A \cap B = \{3, 5, 7\}$, the odd primes. Its complement is the other seven numbers: $\{1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10\}$. By De Morgan that is $A^c \cup B^c$.

items.title: Is it a function
items.prose: A relation from $\{p, q, r\}$ to $\{1, 2, 3\}$, shaded on the grid.
items.question: Which is right?

options.text: Not a function: output 2 is never used
options.why: You required every output to be used. A function needs one cell per row only.

options.text: Not a function: $q$ and $r$ share output 3
options.why: Sharing an output is allowed. One input with two outputs is what breaks it.
You gave the codomain. Output 2 is never reached.

feedback.correct: Right. One cell per row, and outputs 1 and 3 are reached.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells in each row, then list the columns used.

explain.text: Each row has exactly one shaded cell, so this is a function. The shaded columns are 1 and 3, so the image is $\{1, 3\}$. The codomain $\{1, 2, 3\}$ is bigger.

items.title: Neither desk
items.prose: A firm has 30 traders. 18 trade rates, 15 trade FX, and 7 trade both.
items.question: How many trade neither rates nor FX?

feedback.correct: Right. $18 + 15 - 7 = 26$ trade at least one, so 4 trade neither.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the union first, then its complement in the 30.

byKey.union: You found the union, 26. Neither is $30 - 26$.
byKey.no-add: You subtracted 18 and 15 without adding back the 7 counted twice.
byKey.sub-both: You subtracted the 7 as well. It must be added back, not taken away.

explain.text: $|R \cup F| = 18 + 15 - 7 = 26$. Neither is the complement of the union, so $30 - 26 = 4$. That is $R^c \cap F^c$ by De Morgan.

items.title: One-to-one or onto
items.prose: A function from $\{a, b, c, d\}$ to $\{x, y, z\}$, drawn as arrows.
items.question: Which describes it?

options.why: You missed the shared output. $b$ and $d$ both go to $y$.
Every output has an arrow, so it is onto. And $b$, $d$ share $y$.
Every output is reached, so it is onto.

feedback.correct: Right. Every output is hit, but $y$ is hit twice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check outputs for no arrow, and for two arrows.

explain.text: $x$, $y$ and $z$ each receive an arrow, so it is onto. $f(b) = f(d) = y$ with $b \ne d$, so it is not one-to-one. Four inputs into three outputs could never be one-to-one.

items.title: A subset proof
items.prose: Claim: every multiple of 4 is even. That is, $\{n \in \mathbb{Z} : 4 \text{ divides } n\} \subseteq \{n \in \mathbb{Z} : n \text{ is even}\}$.
items.question: Put the proof in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $x$ be any multiple of 4, so $x = 4k$ for some integer $k$.
So $x$ is even. As $x$ was any multiple of 4, the subset holds. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: Examples check two elements. The proof needs an arbitrary multiple of 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from any multiple of 4 and rewrite it.

byKey.d1: You kept the examples. Two cases do not cover every multiple of 4.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: We took any $x = 4k$ and wrote it as $2(2k)$, with $2k$ an integer. That is the definition of even, so $x$ is even. Because $k$ was arbitrary, every multiple of 4 is covered.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $2x - 6 = y$ for $x$, undoing the last step first.

byKey.order: You divided before adding 6. Undo the $-6$ first.

explain.text: From $2x - 6 = y$, add 6 to get $2x = y + 6$, then divide by 2. So $h^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{y + 6}{2}$. Check: $h^{-1}(4) = 5$ and $h(5) = 4$.

items.title: Counting
items.prose: A desk assigns 2 analysts to 5 projects, one project each.
items.question: How many one-to-one assignments are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The second analyst cannot take the first one's project.

byKey.all: You allowed sharing: $5^2 = 25$ counts every function.
byKey.choose: You counted pairs of projects, $\binom{5}{2}$. Which analyst gets which also matters.
byKey.swap: You computed $2^5$, the wrong way round.

explain.text: The first analyst has 5 projects, the second the other 4. So there are $5 \times 4 = 20$ one-to-one functions. None is onto: 2 inputs cannot reach 5 outputs.
